continuity_scope: Bounded tradition-level orientation, not a fictional mega-continuity. Selected literary witness: the sixteenth-century Chinese vernacular novel 西遊記 (Xīyóujì, Journey to the West), represented through Anthony C. Yu's scholarly revised English translation (University of Chicago Press, 2012), Volume 1. The witness is representative of a major premodern Chinese fantastic/religious-literary tradition relevant to later immortal/cultivation imaginaries, but it is not exhaustive of Daoist religious practice, Chinese literature, modern xianxia web fiction, wuxia, games, or any single cultivation system.

work_or_witnesses.work: 西遊記 (Xīyóujì; Journey to the West)
work_or_witnesses.edition: Sixteenth-century Chinese vernacular novel; The Journey to the West, Revised Edition, Vol. 1, translated and edited by Anthony C. Yu, University of Chicago Press, 2012

work_or_witnesses.work: Traditional Chinese Fiction—The State of the Field
work_or_witnesses.edition: Robert E. Hegel, Journal of Asian Studies 53.2 (1994), scholarly context

coverage_rule: Include only the three named central dramatic exemplars directly identified in Yu's Volume 1 description and chapter contents: Xuanzang/Tripitaka, Sun Wukong/Pilgrim Sun, and Zhu Bajie/Eight Rules. Cultivation stages, xian/immortal categories, qi, dantian, sect roles, techniques, talismans, alchemy, tribulations, realms, artifacts, and philosophical/religious terms are source terms or explicit evidence boundaries, never character nodes.
omissions: All other Journey to the West figures, because this is a small orientation sample rather than a complete witness catalog.
Daoist religious practitioners, deities, ritual communities, and philosophical terms as generic fictional character nodes.
Modern xianxia web-fiction characters/conventions, wuxia characters/conventions, and game/system characters.
Cultivation-stage, qi, dantian, sect, technique, talisman, alchemy, tribulation, realm, artifact, and immortal-category nodes.
content_cautions: Journey to the West is a Chinese literary classic deeply entangled with Buddhist, Daoist, and popular religious materials. Terms are not flattened into game classes, moral alignments, or generic fantasy races.

Chinese script and pinyin are supplied only for the selected witness title and named figures where standard transliteration is directly tied to Yu's translation; translation choices remain edition-specific.
Modern xianxia and cultivation vocabulary is heterogeneous. Absence from this single witness is not evidence of absence from Chinese traditions or later genres.
uncertainties: Yu's publisher page provides scholarly bibliographic context and Volume 1 chapter-title evidence, not the complete Chinese text on this page; narrow character claims use the work/translation reference and chapter locators.
The label xianxia is a modern genre label and must not be projected backward as an exact historical category for Journey to the West.
No claim is made that Daoist cultivation, Buddhist doctrine, wuxia, web fiction, or game mechanics are interchangeable.
evidence_basis: University of Chicago Press identifies Yu's complete scholarly translation, the novel's sixteenth-century Chinese context, Xuanzang's pilgrimage, supernatural disciples, and Volume 1 chapter titles naming Sun and Eight Rules. Cambridge's scholarly context cautions against treating Chinese fiction categories as uniform. No fan wiki or Wikipedia was used.

supports: Sixteenth-century Chinese literary witness, Yu translation, Xuanzang and supernatural disciples, and named Sun/Eight Rules chapter evidence.
Scholarly caution that Chinese fiction categories are historically diverse and not uniform.
